title: Lowering the implementation barrier of neutral-atom quantum computing with agentic workflows
authors: Constantin Dalyac, Alexandre Dauphin, Loïc Henriet, Christophe Jurczak
abstract: Quantum computers are moving from research laboratories to industrial machines accessible via the cloud and integrated into high-performance computing facilities. However, translating theoretical quantum protocols into hardware experiments remains a major bottleneck, requiring expertise across protocol design, compilation, simulation, and cloud execution. Here, we introduce an agentic workflow that automates this pipeline on neutral-atom quantum processors (here two Pasqal QPUs available on the cloud) while keeping the researcher in the loop for critical validation. In three case studies from many-body physics and optimization, the agent went from published paper or patent to a QPU campaign run overnight. In particular, human intervention was crucial to ensure scientific validity: the agent selected an inadequate observable in one experiment and constructed a plausible but incorrect hardware diagnosis in another, with both failures detected only through domain-expert review. Finally, we use a second agent to classify a corpus of 633 Rydberg-array arXiv papers and show that nearly half are implementable on present-day QPUs while identifying specific hardware upgrades needed for the rest. Together, these results demonstrate that agentic workflows provide a practical bridge between theoretical ideas and physical hardware, opening quantum experimentation to a much broader scientific community.
summary: The paper introduces an agentic workflow designed to automate the complex process of turning theoretical quantum protocols into executable experiments on neutral-atom quantum processors. By successfully running multiple case studies and screening hundreds of papers, it proves that AI tools can bridge the gap between theory and hardware. This significantly lowers the barrier for researchers in AMO physics to conduct cutting-edge quantum simulations.
main_problem: The major bottleneck in quantum research is translating theoretical protocols into executable hardware experiments due to required expertise across multiple domains.
main_result: Agentic workflows provide a practical bridge by automating the pipeline from scientific paper to QPU campaign, significantly accelerating the path from theory to physical realization.
method: The authors developed and demonstrated an agentic workflow that automates protocol extraction, hardware mapping, simulation (noiseless/noise-aware), and execution on neutral-atom quantum processors.
model_or_system: The work focuses on neutral-atom Quantum Processing Units (QPUs) utilizing Rydberg arrays to realize programmable many-body Hamiltonians. The system is controlled by parameters like Rabi frequency, detuning, and qubit geometry.
key_observables: Density-density correlator G(r), structure factor, mean magnetization m, and comparison of measured data against noiseless simulation envelopes.
important_parameters: Device constraints include maximum atom number, achievable detuning range ($	ext{FC1}: |\delta|/2\pi \le 10 	ext{ MHz}$), and interaction types (e.g., Ising vs XY).
main_assumptions: Human domain expertise remains crucial for validating scientific assumptions, selecting physically meaningful observables, and interpreting complex results.
figures_summary: Figure 2 compares literature values of the density-density correlator G(r) with measurements on FC1 and SA1 for the $Z_2$ phase. Figure 3 (mentioned) compares QMC data to QPU data for the $1/3$ plateau.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the agentic workflow, demonstrates its use in three case studies from literature (many-body physics and optimization), details the process of screening existing arXiv papers, and concludes by outlining the shift in the research bottleneck to scientific judgment.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the practical implementation gap for AMO theorists. By automating the engineering steps—from protocol extraction to noise modeling on specific hardware like Pasqal QPUs—it allows theorists to rapidly test feasibility across a much broader range of physical models.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. AI-assisted workflow for translating quantum protocols into hardware experiments. A researcher defines the scientific objective and interacts with the AI workflow through natural-language instructions. The AI extracts or generates an experimental protocol, including the neutral-atom register and pulse sequence, from a scientific publication, patent, or user request. The pulse sequence is determined by the qubit register, the time evolution of the Rabi frequency Ω(rad.µs−1) and the detuning δ (rad.µs−1).
